common_name: Livingston's Paragon Tomato (1870 Foundational Smooth-Skinned Heirloom)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Paragon is a vigorous indeterminate regular-leaf variety that benefits from staking to keep the abundant medium-round fruit off the ground.

directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm, fertile soil once frost danger has passed, staking to support the heavy fruit set. Introduced by Ohio seedsman Alexander W. Livingston in 1870, Paragon is historically significant as the first tomato widely recognized for producing smooth, uniformly round, evenly red fruit without the deep ridges and cracking typical of tomatoes at the time, a breakthrough that helped popularize the tomato as a garden and market crop across 19th-century America. The plants are productive and disease-tolerant for an heirloom, yielding clusters of medium-sized red fruit with classic old-fashioned flavor suited to fresh eating and canning.

common_name: Golden Queen Tomato (Livingston's 1882 Smooth Yellow Heirloom)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Golden Queen is an indeterminate regular-leaf variety that needs staking or caging to support its large smooth fruit.

directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil, staking the vigorous vines to support fruit. Released by Livingston Seed Company in 1882, Golden Queen was long marketed as the finest smooth yellow tomato available, producing large, 8-12 ounce, waxy golden-yellow fruit that is sometimes blushed with pink at the blossom end, with meaty, low-seed flesh and a mild, sweet flavor that made it a favorite among 19th- and early 20th-century home gardeners seeking a low-acid alternative to red slicers.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Purple Calabash is a sprawling indeterminate variety that needs sturdy staking or caging, and its heavily ruffled fruit benefits from good airflow to reduce rot in the folds.

directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm, fertile soil, staking well to support the sprawling vines. One of the oldest known tomato heirlooms, Purple Calabash produces small to medium, deeply ruffled and pleated fruit that ranges from dusky pink-burgundy to dark purple-brown, believed to closely resemble tomatoes as they looked before generations of breeding smoothed and enlarged the fruit. The flesh is complex and tangy with a distinctive rich flavor, and the variety was preserved and distributed through Seed Savers Exchange in the early 1990s.

common_name: Brimmer Tomato (Wood's Famous 1907 Virginia Heirloom Beefsteak)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Brimmer is a vigorous indeterminate variety that requires sturdy staking or caging to support its very heavy, often one- to two-pound fruit.

directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into deeply worked, fertile soil, staking firmly to bear the weight of the fruit. Developed in the early 1900s by a Richmond, Virginia seed company, Brimmer, marketed historically as Wood's Famous Brimmer, won a Grand Prize in 1907 for its large, round, pink-to-purple fruit that is thick-skinned, meaty, and low-acid, often exceeding a pound at full size. The variety fell out of commercial favor by the mid-1960s but has since been preserved and revived by regional seed savers, including Southern Exposure Seed Exchange.

common_name: German Red Strawberry Tomato (Heart-Shaped German Oxheart Heirloom)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; German Red Strawberry is a vigorous indeterminate variety reaching 5-7 feet that needs sturdy staking or caging to support its large heart-shaped fruit.

directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil, staking well as vines can reach 5-7 feet. German Red Strawberry is a German oxheart heirloom prized for its large, strawberry- or heart-shaped fruit, typically 3-4 inches long and 10-16 ounces, that ripens to a deep red with smooth shoulders and thick, meaty, relatively low-seed flesh. The flavor is rich and well-balanced with classic old-fashioned sweetness, making it popular for slicing as well as sauce, though fruit shape can be somewhat variable from plant to plant.

common_name: Old Ivory Egg Tomato (Pale Ivory Egg-Shaped Heirloom)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Old Ivory Egg is a highly productive indeterminate variety that benefits from staking or caging to manage prolific small egg-shaped fruit clusters.

directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm, fertile soil, staking to support the abundant fruit set. Old Ivory Egg produces small, egg-shaped, 2-3 ounce fruit that ripens from pale ivory to a soft creamy yellow, with a mild, sweet flavor carrying a hint of citrus, and is prized for its striking pale coloring in salads and mixed cherry-tomato plates. The variety was distributed in a mid-1980s Seed Savers Exchange yearbook by a Wisconsin member who traced the seed stock back to Australia.

common_name: Trucker's Favorite Tomato (Pre-1900 New Jersey Heirloom Pink Slicer)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Trucker's Favorite is a vigorous indeterminate variety with good foliage disease tolerance that still benefits from staking to keep fruit clusters off the ground.

directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil, staking to support the vigorous vines. Trucker's Favorite is a pre-1900 heirloom traced to Burlington County, New Jersey and offered commercially by W. Atlee Burpee before 1899; it was named for its popularity among market gardeners hauling produce to city markets. The plants set clusters of 3-4 crack-resistant, 6-12 ounce pink beefsteak-type fruit with a rich, sweet, old-fashioned flavor and notably good foliage disease resistance for an heirloom of its era.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Stone is a vigorous indeterminate regular-leaf variety with above-average foliage disease tolerance for an heirloom, but still benefits from staking.

directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile soil, staking the vigorous vines. Introduced by Livingston Seed Company in 1889 from a market grower's field near Grandville, Ohio, Stone produces dense, heavy, 6-8 ounce red fruit with an old-fashioned tangy acidity that made it a favorite for canning, juice, catsup, and chili sauce in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Its name references the notable density and weight of its fruit compared to other varieties of the period, and the plants show better foliage disease resistance than many contemporaries.

common_name: Lillian's Yellow Heirloom Tomato (Pale Yellow Tennessee Potato-Leaf Beefsteak)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Lillian's Yellow is a tall, late-season potato-leaf indeterminate that needs a long, warm growing season and sturdy staking for its large fruit.

directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm, fertile soil, staking to support the tall, vigorous potato-leaf vines. Lillian's Yellow was collected from a Tennessee grower and passed on for distribution through a Seed Savers Exchange yearbook; it requires a long season, typically 90-100 days from transplant, to produce its large, 12-20 ounce, pale yellow fruit that is sometimes blushed pink at the blossom end. The meaty, low-seed flesh is prized among heirloom growers as one of the finest-tasting yellow tomatoes, with a mild, citrusy sweetness distinct from more golden-orange yellow varieties.

common_name: Yellow Bell Tomato (Appalachian Heirloom Yellow Paste Tomato)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Yellow Bell is a heavy-yielding indeterminate paste tomato that tolerates cool, wet conditions better than many sauce varieties and benefits from staking or caging.

directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile soil, staking or caging to support heavy clusters of fruit. Yellow Bell is a Roma-shaped yellow paste tomato that is a family heirloom from Tennessee, introduced commercially in 1986 by Southern Exposure Seed Exchange; the vigorous plants set 5-12 fruits per cluster and bear heavily until frost, ripening from green through creamy yellow to a rich golden-yellow with a sweet, full flavor well suited to yellow sauces, salsas, preserves, and catsup.

common_name: Watermelon Beefsteak Tomato (West Virginia Heirloom Pink Beefsteak)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Watermelon Beefsteak is a large-fruited indeterminate variety that needs sturdy staking or caging to support fruit that can reach 1-2 pounds.

directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into deeply worked, fertile soil, staking firmly to support the very heavy fruit. Watermelon Beefsteak is a West Virginia heirloom dating to the 1800s, later listed in a 1958 seed catalog, that produces huge, pink-skinned beefsteak fruit with purplish-red flesh reminiscent of watermelon coloring, weighing up to 1-2 pounds at maturity. The flavor is mild, juicy, and sweet, and the large flattened fruit is prized for slicing into broad rounds for sandwiches and salads.
